title: BFS shortest path guarantee condition
prompt_markdown: Under what condition is Breadth-First Search (BFS) guaranteed to find the shortest path between two vertices?

choices: In any graph where all edges have equal non-negative weight (unweighted)
Only if the graph has no cycles and is a binary tree
Only if edge weights are negative
content.explanation: BFS explores vertices in order of layer distance (1 step, 2 steps, etc.). Therefore, in an unweighted graph where every edge has equal cost, the first time target is reached is guaranteed to be the shortest path.

title: Timing of visited set marking
prompt_markdown: Why must a neighbor node be added to the `visited` set immediately upon being *enqueued*, rather than waiting until it is *dequeued*?
hints: What happens if two parent nodes share the same unvisited neighbor?

choices: To satisfy Python interpreter syntax requirements
To prevent other concurrently processed nodes from enqueuing the exact same neighbor multiple times
Because Python deques cannot store unvisited elements
content.explanation: If node C is a neighbor of both A and B, and A enqueues C without marking it visited, B will also enqueue C. Marking visited upon enqueuing guarantees each node enters the queue exactly once.

title: BFS time complexity on graph
prompt_markdown: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search on a graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges represented as an adjacency list?
hints: Every vertex is enqueued once; every edge is inspected once.

content.explanation: BFS visits every reachable vertex once (O(V)) and scans each outgoing edge in the adjacency list once (O(E)), resulting in O(V + E) overall runtime.

title: Predict layer-by-layer exploration order
prompt_markdown: Given undirected graph: `0 -- 1`, `0 -- 2`, `1 -- 3`, `2 -- 3`, `2 -- 4`. Trace the nodes processed in each distance layer when BFS starts at node 0.
hints: Distance 0: {0}. Neighbors of 0 are distance 1. Neighbors of distance 1 are distance 2.

rubric: Correctly notes that node 3 is visited from layer 1 and not re-added when exploring node 2
content.reference_answer:
Layer Trace:
- Layer 0 (Distance 0): `[0]`
- Layer 1 (Distance 1): `[1, 2]` (direct neighbors of 0)
- Layer 2 (Distance 2): `[3, 4]` (3 is neighbor of 1 and 2; 4 is neighbor of 2)
Resulting layer grouping: `[[0], [1, 2], [3, 4]]`.

title: Fix O(n^2) list pop performance trap in BFS

rubric: Explains that `queue.pop(0)` takes O(N) time on a list, shifting elements and making BFS quadratic O(V^2 + E)
Achieves true O(V + E) linear runtime

title: Implement multi-source BFS for Rotting Oranges
prompt_markdown: Write a Python function `oranges_rotting(grid: list[list[int]]) -> int` that calculates the minimum minutes until no fresh orange (1) remains adjacent to a rotten orange (2). Empty cells are 0. Use multi-source BFS.
hints: Enqueue all initially rotten oranges (2). Track count of fresh oranges (1). Decrement fresh on infection.

rubric: Finds all rotten oranges (value 2) and enqueues them in queue
Executes multi-source BFS layer-by-layer, converting adjacent fresh oranges to rotten

title: Explain bidirectional BFS in interviews
prompt_markdown: In a system design or algorithmic interview for Word Ladder or route planning, the interviewer asks: 'Standard BFS runs out of memory on large graphs. How does Bi-directional BFS reduce memory and time complexity?' Provide a mathematical explanation.
hints: Compare branching factor b^d vs 2 * b^(d/2).

rubric: Defines Bi-directional BFS: searches simultaneously forward from start and backward from target
Explains the frontier meeting condition: stops when the forward and backward frontiers intersect
Analyzes complexity difference: branching factor b to depth d takes O(b^d) nodes; bi-directional meets at d/2, taking O(2 * b^(d/2))
Gives concrete numeric comparison (e.g. b=10, d=6 -> 1,000,000 nodes vs 2,000 nodes)
content.reference_answer:
1. Core Mechanism:
Instead of expanding a single BFS tree from `start` all the way to `target` across depth $d$, Bi-directional BFS maintains two simultaneous frontiers:
- Forward frontier originating from `start`
- Backward frontier originating from `target`
At each step, expand the smaller of the two frontiers. When an expanded node intersects with the opposing visited set, the shortest path is found.

2. Mathematical Complexity Reduction:
Assume every node has an average branching factor of $b$ neighbors, and the shortest path has distance $d$.
- Standard BFS explores nodes down to depth $d$:
  $$\text{Total Nodes} = b^0 + b^1 + \dots + b^d \approx O(b^d)$$
- Bi-directional BFS expands both trees only to the midpoint depth $d / 2$:
  $$\text{Total Nodes} = 2 \times O(b^{d/2})$$

3. Practical Impact:
If branching factor $b = 10$ and distance $d = 6$:
- Standard BFS must explore $10^6 = 1,000,000$ states (frequently causing Out-Of-Memory errors).
- Bi-directional BFS explores $2 \times 10^3 = 2,000$ states!
This cuts search space and memory consumption by several orders of magnitude.
